newsitem.title: USA: UPS Teamster strike could fog US economic readings.
newsitem.headline: UPS Teamster strike could fog US economic readings.

text.p: A strike at United Parcel Service, the nation's largest package delivery service, is likely to fog upcoming U.S. economic data and a prolonged work stoppage could actually slow U.S. growth, economists said.

"The strike ultimately could delay a lot of shipments and it could have some economic impact," said Elliott Platt, managing director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. "How severe the impact is depends on the longevity of the strike."

The Teamsters union went on strike at UPS on Monday. Striking drivers, package-sorters and loaders shut down UPS facilities after midnight on Sunday, hours after talks between the union and UPS management collapsed.
UPS handles 12 million packages a day, or about 80 percent of domestic parcel deliveries. It employs 301,000 workers in the United States, 185,000 of them Teamsters.
One of the first measures of economic activity that could feel the impact of the UPS strike is the weekly jobless claims data.
Strikers generally are not entitled to unemployment benefits. But anyone on the periphery of the strike who is laid off because of it can file for unemployment benefits.
Besides the jobless claims, another gauge likely to feel the UPS strike is the supplier delivery item of the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index.
"You would see the purchasing managers reporting that they were getting deliveries at a slower pace," said Platt.

Lengthening supplier delivery times are usually interpreted as signs of bottlenecks in the economy that can develop when demand for goods is increasing enough to put pressure on the ability of suppliers to deliver them.

Such bottlenecks can be seen as forerunners of inflation pressures. If supplier delivery times suddenly were to lengthen sharply, "you'd have to discount this" as being tied to the strike by the giant delivery service, Platt said.
William Dudley, managing director and head of economic research at Goldman, Sachs & Co Inc, agreed.

"This will make people fairly suspect about a lot of these numbers. You wouldn't know if bottlenecks are being caused by a strong economy or because the strike is drawing out the time it takes to deliver things," he said. "People will tend to discount the numbers.
"Then when the strike ends, you could have a surge in activity and people will have a hard time figuring what that means," Dudley said.
Some reactions to the strike might counter-balance each other, economists said.
"Some people might delay buying things because they're not sure how long it will take them to receive them," said Dudley.
On the other hand, some people might order items early in order to allow extra time for delivery.
The strike could cause short-run production adjustments, said Dudley. And inventories might rise a little bit.

"Virtually all the economic activity indicators could be affected to some extent (by the strike)," said David Sloan, senior economist at I.D.E.A. "Most of the statistics are at risk of some distortions."
Sloan said the strike could impact the monthly employment figures, the shipment components of the purchasing managers indices and consumer spending.
If supplier delivery times lengthen, it will be hard to decipher how much of that is due to the strike, he said.
"The strike probably will dampen everything to some extent," said Sloan. "But it's difficult to say by how much."
